instructions: This test consists of 60 items. You will have 1 hour and 15 minutes to answer them.
In addition to this test booklet, you should have an answer sheet.
Each item in this test has four suggested answers lettered (A), (B), (C), (D). Read each item you are about to answer and decide which choice is best.
On your answer sheet, find the number which corresponds to your item and shade the space having the same letter as the answer you have chosen.
If you want to change your answer, erase it completely before you fill in your new choice.
When you are told to begin, turn the page and work as quickly and as carefully as you can. If you cannot answer an item, go on to the next one. You may return to that item later.
You may do any rough work in this booklet.
Figures are not necessarily drawn to scale.
You may use a silent, non-programmable calculator to answer items.

items.stem: A student measures the time for 20 complete swings as 36.0 s. The period of the pendulum, in s, is

misconception.label: Divided the number of swings by the time instead of the time by the number of swings.
Divided by 10 rather than by 20.
Multiplied the time by the number of swings instead of dividing.

steps: The period T is the time taken for one complete oscillation.
Twenty oscillations take 36.0 s.
T = 36.0 ÷ 20 = 1.80 s. Timing many swings and dividing is what keeps the reaction time error small.

items.objective_statement: discuss possible types and sources of error in any measurement
items.stem: A student always starts a stopwatch slightly late. This is an example of

misconception.label: A random error scatters readings both ways.
A zero error is an instrument reading a value when it should read zero.
An anomalous result is a single reading far from the rest.

steps: Random errors scatter readings above and below the true value, and averaging reduces them.
An error that is always in the same direction shifts every reading the same way.
That is a systematic error, and averaging does not remove it.

items.objective_statement: apply the principle of moments
items.stem: For a body acted on by several forces to be in equilibrium, it is necessary that the

options.text: forces are all equal in size

misconception.label: The forces need not be equal, only balanced.

options.text: resultant force is zero and the resultant moment is zero
forces all act at the same point

misconception.label: Forces may act at different points, which is why the moment condition is needed.
A body moving at constant velocity is also in equilibrium.

steps: If the resultant force were not zero, the body would accelerate.
If the resultant moment were not zero, the body would start to rotate.
Both conditions are therefore needed.
solution.answer_line: resultant force is zero and the resultant moment is zero

items.objective_statement: explain the action of common tools and devices as levers
items.stem: A pair of scissors is an example of a

misconception.label: A pulley turns a rope round a wheel to change the direction of a force.

items.objective_statement: solve problems using Hooke’s law
items.stem: Hooke's law states that the extension of a spring is

misconception.label: Extension and force are different quantities and cannot be equal.

options.text: proportional to the force applied, up to a limit
inversely proportional to the force applied

misconception.label: A larger force gives a larger extension, not a smaller one.

misconception.label: Mass times acceleration is the resultant force.

items.objective_statement: describe situations that demonstrate the law of conservation of linear momentum
items.stem: When a gun is fired, the gun recoils. This is a demonstration of the

misconception.label: Energy is not conserved in the useful sense here; chemical energy is released.
The principle of moments concerns turning effects.
Gravitation is not involved in the recoil.

steps: Before firing, the gun and bullet are at rest, so the total momentum is zero.
No external horizontal force acts, so the total momentum stays zero.
The bullet's forward momentum must therefore be balanced by the gun's backward momentum.

items.objective_statement: explain the term efficiency
items.stem: No machine can have an efficiency of 100 per cent because

options.text: energy is destroyed inside the machine

misconception.label: Energy is never destroyed; it changes form.

options.text: some energy is always transferred to forms that are not useful
the machine creates energy as it works

misconception.label: A machine cannot create energy.

options.text: the input energy is always smaller than the output energy

misconception.label: The input is always the larger of the two.

steps: Efficiency is the useful output energy divided by the total input energy.
Friction and air resistance always transfer some of the input to thermal energy and sound.
That energy is not useful output, so the efficiency is always below 100 per cent.
solution.answer_line: some energy is always transferred to forms that are not useful

items.objective_statement: distinguish among solids, liquids and gases
items.stem: Compared with the particles of a solid, the particles of the same substance as a gas are

options.text: much closer together and moving more slowly

misconception.label: This describes going the other way, from gas to solid.

options.text: much further apart and moving much faster
the same distance apart but moving faster

misconception.label: The spacing increases greatly; a gas occupies roughly a thousand times the volume.

options.text: much further apart and moving more slowly

misconception.label: Gas particles move faster, not slower; the higher temperature means more kinetic energy.

steps: Energy supplied in melting and boiling pulls the particles apart against the forces holding them.
Further energy raises the average kinetic energy, so the particles move faster.
So a gas has particles both further apart and faster than the solid.
solution.answer_line: much further apart and moving much faster

steps: Fixed volume means the particles are close together and cannot move apart.
No fixed shape means they are free to move past one another.
Both together describe a liquid.
solution.answer_line: a liquid

misconception.label: Current carried depends on the cable's cross section, not its sag.

options.text: the sag keeps the cable further from the ground

misconception.label: Sagging brings the middle of the cable closer to the ground, not further.

misconception.label: Resistance depends on length and thickness; sagging does not lower it.

steps: Metals contract when they cool.

Leaving it slack in warm weather means the cold weather tension stays safe.
